summary: Describes a historical method for carrying SONET/SDH signals over packet networks using MPLS and IP. RFC 4842 now covers the standards-track protocol and new implementations should use it. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 4842.

plainLanguage.summary: This is an old way to move telephone-network signals across packet networks. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 4842.

subtitle: An old way to send traditional phone and circuit-switched signals over packet networks

tldr.problem: Telephone networks and private leased lines use SONET and SDH, which are circuit-based and send data at fixed rates. Packet networks are bursty and variable. Network operators needed a way to carry SONET/SDH signals through packet-switched MPLS networks.
tldr.mechanism: The CEM (Circuit Emulation Service) encapsulation breaks SONET/SDH signals into fixed-size packets, adds a 32-bit header with sequence numbers and control bits, and sends them through an MPLS tunnel with VC labels. Dynamic Bandwidth Allocation can save bandwidth during idle periods by sending only headers.
tldr.outcome: This design allowed traditional TDM circuits to work over packet networks. RFC 4842 later superseded this document with a standards-track version, and new implementations must use RFC 4842 instead. RFC 5143 is Historic.

facts.label: Structure Pointer range
facts.value: 0 to 1022 (0x3FF when J1 byte not present)

facts.label: Minimum payload length
facts.value: 261 bytes for structured CEM with pointer adjustments

today: RFC 5143 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 4842, which defines the standards-track Circuit Emulation over Packet (CEP) protocol. RFC 5143 serves as documentation only; new implementations must use RFC 4842.

sections.title: Emulating Circuits Over Packets
sections.content:
RFC 5143 describes Circuit Emulation Service (CEM), a historical method for carrying SONET and SDH signals (used in traditional telephone and private leased-line networks) across packet-switched networks using MPLS. SONET (Synchronous Optical Network) is used in North America; SDH (Synchronous Digital Hierarchy) is the international equivalent.

Traditional circuit networks send data at fixed rates with guaranteed timing. Packet networks send variable-sized bursts. CEM makes the packet network appear like a circuit network to the user. The RFC covers multiple SONET/SDH rates (STS-1 through STS-192c / VC-3 through VC-4-64c), both structured emulation (individual channels) and unstructured emulation (entire bit-stream), and an optional Dynamic Bandwidth Allocation (DBA) mode that saves bandwidth during idle periods.
sections.plainLanguage: Telephone networks send voice and data in a steady stream. This RFC shows how to send that steady stream through a packet network (like the Internet) that normally sends bursts of variable size.

sections.title: The CEM Header
sections.content:
Every CEM packet begins with a 32-bit header containing several fields. The D bit signals whether Dynamic Bandwidth Allocation is active. The R bit (CEM-RDI) indicates loss of packet synchronization. A sequence number (10 bits, cycling 0-1023) allows detection of lost and reordered packets. The Structure Pointer holds the offset of the J1 byte in the SONET/SDH payload, helping reconstruct the signal's timing alignment.

The N and P bits signal pointer adjustment events in structured mode, or AIS-P (Alarm Indication Signal - Path) when both are set to one. Finally, a 6-bit ECC-6 error correction code protects the header itself, providing single-bit correction and detection of up to two bit errors.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is like a label on each packet: sequence number (is this packet #5?), timing information (where in the original signal is this?), and an error check to spot corruption.

sections.title: CEM Modes and Operation
sections.content:
Structured CEM terminates the SONET/SDH transport overhead and packetizes individual channels, and is required to be supported. Unstructured CEM packetizes the entire SONET/SDH bit-stream including transport overhead, and is optional.

In normal mode, SONET/SDH payloads are fragmented into fixed-size packets, each with the CEM header and VC label. Dynamic Bandwidth Allocation (DBA) is an optional extension where during idle periods (such as AIS-P or STS SPE Unequipped), only the header and labels are sent, omitting the payload. This reduces bandwidth usage during such conditions. Both structured and unstructured CEM use MPLS tunnel and VC labels to route and identify the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal mode sends a steady stream of packets with timing information in each one. DBA mode is smarter: when there is nothing useful to send (like during a disconnected phone line), it only sends the header, saving bandwidth.

sections.title: Clock Recovery and Synchronization
sections.content:
CEM supports two clocking modes to regenerate the original SONET/SDH clock rate at the receiver. Synchronous mode is used when both ends have access to the same external clock source; the receiver simply clocks data out at the fixed rate and uses the N and P bits to replay pointer adjustment events.

Asynchronous mode is used when synchronous timing is unavailable. The receiver must employ adaptive clock recovery techniques to regenerate the clock from the arriving packet stream. In this mode, the CEM de-packetizer may calculate its own pointer adjustments to align the received SPE with the outgoing SONET/SDH transport framing.
sections.plainLanguage: Synchronous mode: both sides have a clock that ticks at the same rate, so just play out the data steadily. Asynchronous mode: figure out the right speed from watching the packets arrive.

sections.title: Historical Status
sections.content: RFC 5143 is Historic. RFC 4842, published around the same time, describes the standards-track protocol for CEM and must be used for new implementations. The main difference is that RFC 4842 avoids a potential ambiguity in the CEM header that could cause MPLS networks to misinterpret certain packets when Equal Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing is in use. RFC 5143 serves as documentation of existing implementations built to this earlier design.
sections.plainLanguage: This was an early, working design that got used in real networks. But there is now a better, cleaner standard version (RFC 4842) that fixes a subtle issue and should be used for anything new.
